subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Food Security, Food Safety & Food Processing

subjective.question: What are probiotics?
subjective.answer: Probiotics are live bacteria and yeasts that are good for your health, especially your digestive system. We usually think of bacteria as something that causes diseases, but your body is full of bacteria, both good and bad. Probiotics are often called "good" or "helpful" bacteria because they help keep your gut healthy. Good bacteria are naturally found in your body, and probiotics can also be found in some foods and supplements.

subjective.question: What are the types of probiotics?
subjective.answer: Many types of bacteria are classified as probiotics. They all have different benefits, but most come from two groups. Lactobacillus: this may be the most common probiotic; it is the one found in yogurt and other fermented foods. Different strains can help with diarrhea and may help people who can't digest lactose, the sugar in milk. Bifidobacterium: it is also found in some dairy products and may help ease the symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and some other conditions. Saccharomyces boulardii is a yeast found in probiotics; it appears to help fight diarrhea and other digestive problems.

subjective.question: What do probiotics do?
subjective.answer: Probiotics help move food through your gut. Researchers are still trying to figure out which are best for certain health problems. Some common conditions they treat are: irritable bowel syndrome; inflammatory bowel disease (IBD); infectious diarrhea (caused by viruses, bacteria, or parasites); and antibiotic-related diarrhea. There is also some research to show they help with problems in other parts of your body, for example skin conditions like eczema, urinary and vaginal health, preventing allergies and colds, and oral health.

subjective.topic: Food Security, Food Safety & Food Processing
subjective.question: Write the names of the four primary food security research needs.
subjective.answer: The four primary food security research needs are: (1) Prevention ("Shields") - inactivation/neutralization technologies, security technologies and in-line sensors; (2) Response and Recovery - laboratory support, rapid response research team and facility clean-up; (3) Detection Methodology - deployable, rapid field tests, laboratory-based screening tests and laboratory-based confirmatory tests; and (4) Forensics, technology transfer and methods validation.

subjective.topic: Food Security, Food Safety & Food Processing
subjective.question: What is the response and recovery component of primary food security?
subjective.answer: Response and Recovery consists of: laboratory support; a rapid response research team; and facility clean-up.

subjective.topic: Food Security, Food Safety & Food Processing
subjective.question: What is food safety? (What are the potential health risks from food consumption?)
subjective.answer: Food safety is concerned with the potential health risks from food consumption: microbiological, viral and parasitic concerns; hormone residues (growth promoters); and animal drugs (antibiotics).

subjective.topic: Food Security, Food Safety & Food Processing
subjective.question: What are food additives?
subjective.answer: Food additives are substances added to products to perform specific technological functions. These functions include preserving, i.e. increasing shelf-life or inhibiting the growth of pathogens, or adding colouring and flavouring to food for interest and variety. There are over 300 permitted additives that can be used in the UK. Flavourings are not included in this figure, as there are over 3,000 flavouring components in UK use, in many different combinations. International organisations provide advice on the safety of flavourings.

subjective.topic: Food Security, Food Safety & Food Processing
subjective.question: What is steam pasteurization?
subjective.answer: Steam pasteurization is a whole carcass treatment; it brings the surface to about 200°F. It is extremely effective, but expensive and water- and energy-intensive.

subjective.question: What is the relationship of microorganisms with food?
subjective.answer: Microorganisms in food may be: (i) Pathogenic or toxigenic - they cause disease; (ii) Beneficial/desirable - they make food, e.g. Lactobacilli bacteria in fermented food (yoghurt, pickles) and yeast Saccharomyces in bread and baking; (iii) Deteriorated/undesirable - non-pathogenic organisms that cause spoilage, e.g. fungi, Pseudomonas, Proteus and Bacillus. Conditions for spoilage are water, pH, physical structure, oxygen and temperature. Organisms that cause spoilage include Pseudomonas, Proteus, Serratia, Lactobacillus, Micrococcus and fungi such as Aspergillus, Rhizopus and yeast. Spoilage appears as greening, moldy appearance, rotting, discoloration, souring and bad smell.

subjective.question: What is a predominant microorganism?
subjective.answer: Unspoiled, nonsterile food generally contains many types of microorganisms from different genera. When the same food is spoiled, it is found to contain predominantly one or two types, and they may not even be present initially in the highest numbers in the unspoiled fresh product.

subjective.question: Differentiate between food-borne infections and food-borne intoxication.
subjective.answer: Food-borne infections: they are caused by bacteria, viruses or parasites, which invade and/or multiply in the lining of the intestine; the incubation period is hours to days; symptoms are diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps and fever; they are communicable and spread from person to person; contributing factors are inadequate cooking, cross contamination, poor personal hygiene and bare-hand contact. Food-borne intoxications: they are caused by toxins (natural, preformed bacterial or chemical); there is no invasion or multiplication; the incubation period is minutes to hours; symptoms are vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, diplopia, weakness, respiratory failure, numbness and sensory/motor dysfunction; they are not communicable; contributing factors are inadequate cooking and improper handling temperatures.

subjective.question: Name the four types of carbohydrates.
subjective.answer: 1. Monosaccharides 2. Disaccharides 3. Oligosaccharides 4. Polysaccharides

subjective.question: What are reducing disaccharides?
subjective.answer: Reducing disaccharides are those in which one monosaccharide, the reducing sugar of the pair, still has a free hemiacetal unit that can act as a reducing aldehyde group. Examples: cellobiose and maltose.

subjective.question: What is the occurrence of glutamic acid?
subjective.answer: Glutamic acid was first isolated from wheat gluten by Ritthausen in 1866. It is abundant in most proteins, but is particularly high in milk proteins (21.7%), wheat (31.4%), corn (18.4%) and soya (18.5%). Molasses also contains relatively high amounts of glutamic acid.

subjective.question: Write the names of three basic amino acids.
subjective.answer: Lysine, arginine and histidine.

subjective.question: What is a fibrous protein? Write its two examples.
subjective.answer: In fibrous proteins the entire peptide chain is packed or arranged within a single regular structure. Stabilization of these structures is achieved by intermolecular bonding (electrostatic interaction and disulfide linkages, but primarily hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions). Examples: wool keratin (α-helix), silk fibroin (β-sheet structure) and collagen (a triple helix).

subjective.question: What is a beta turn? Describe its types.
subjective.answer: β-turns, also known as β-bends, tight turns or reverse turns, are a type of non-regular secondary structure in proteins that cause a change in direction of the polypeptide chain. They occur at hairpin corners where the peptide chain changes direction abruptly; such corners involve four amino acid residues, often including proline and glycine. Several types of turns are known; of greatest importance are Type I (42% of 421 examined turns), Type II (15%) and Type III (18%). In Type I β-turns all amino acid residues are allowed, with the exception of proline in position 3. In Type II β-turns glycine is required in position 3. In Type III β-turns all amino acids are allowed.

subjective.question: Give the classification of amino acids on the basis of nutrition, with two examples of each type.
subjective.answer: 1. Essential amino acids: these amino acids are not synthesized in the cells of human beings, so they should be essentially present in the diet, e.g. phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, arginine, leucine and lysine. Arginine is a conditional amino acid (essential for infants, non-essential for adults). 2. Non-essential amino acids: these amino acids can be synthesized in the body, so they need not be included in the diet, e.g. glycine, alanine, serine, cysteine, asparagine, glutamine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, tyrosine and proline.

subjective.question: What are the types of secondary structure of protein?
subjective.answer: Alpha helix: in an α-helix, the carbonyl (C=O) of one amino acid is hydrogen bonded to the amino H (N-H) of an amino acid that is four residues down the chain. β-pleated sheet: two or more segments of a polypeptide chain line up next to each other, forming a sheet-like structure held together by hydrogen bonds. The hydrogen bonding in a β-sheet is between strands (inter-strand) rather than within strands (intra-strand).

subjective.question: Which forces give rise to the tertiary structure of a protein?
subjective.answer: The forces that give rise to the tertiary structure of a protein are ionic bonding, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interaction and disulfide bonds.

subjective.question: Define water activity.
subjective.answer: Water activity is "the partial vapor pressure of water in a substance divided by the standard state partial vapor pressure of water": aw = P/P0, where P is the partial vapor pressure of food moisture at temperature T and P0 is the saturation vapor pressure of pure water at T. Pure distilled water has a water activity of exactly one. Higher aw substances tend to support more microorganisms: bacteria usually require at least 0.91, and fungi at least 0.7.

subjective.question: Define nutrition and food technology. What are nutrients?
subjective.answer: The chemical components of food that perform the body functions are called nutrients. Nutrition is the study of various nutrients, their functions, food sources and their utilization by the human body. Food technology is the application of food science and engineering principles to the selection, preservation, processing, packaging, distribution and use of safe, nutritious food. (Facts stated in the lecture file: nutrients perform the functions of food components; about 65 to 80 percent of the energy in our diet is supplied by carbohydrates.)

subjective.question: What does food composition tell us about a food? What are its main components?
subjective.answer: Food composition tells us about the protein, carbohydrates, fat, vitamins and minerals present in a food. Water is the chemical substance found in the largest amount in food: foods contain about 60-95% moisture (milk, for example, has a moisture content of about 87%). Proteins contain about 16% nitrogen, and the human body requires 14 minerals and vitamins (such as A, K, C and the water-soluble B and C vitamins) for proper health and growth.

subjective.question: Describe fats and oils: how are they built, and what are their energy value, specific gravity, smoke point and emulsification?
subjective.answer: Fats are built up by linking together a number of individual fatty acids with glycerol. Each gram of pure fat or oil supplies nine kilocalories, so fats are a concentrated form of energy. The specific gravity of oils and fats is about 0.9. The smoke point is the temperature at which a fat or oil gives off a thin bluish smoke. Lipids can form an emulsion with water when beaten up with it to form tiny globules in the presence of a suitable emulsifying agent; this is called emulsification.

subjective.question: What is rancidity of fats? Describe its types.
subjective.answer: Spoilage of fats results in off flavour and renders the fat inedible; these changes are known as rancidity of fats. In hydrolytic rancidity, hydrolysis decomposes the fats (triglyceride molecules) into glycerol and free fatty acids. Oxidation of unsaturated fats leads to oxidative rancidity. The iodine number of a fat is a measure of its degree of unsaturation, i.e. the number of carbon double bonds in relation to the amount of fat or oil.

subjective.question: What is hydrogenation of oils? State the conditions required for it.
subjective.answer: Hydrogenation is the process in which oils are exposed to hydrogen gas under conditions of high temperature (150-180°C) and pressure (2-10 atm) in the presence of a nickel catalyst, which hardens the oil by saturating its double bonds.

subjective.question: Compare the methods of pasteurization of milk. What is the shelf life of pasteurized milk?
subjective.answer: Holding method: milk is held at 62.7°C for 30 minutes. Higher Temperature Short Time (HTST) method: milk is heated to 71.6°C for at least 15 seconds. Ultra High Temperature (UHT) process: milk is heated to 132°C for one second and then packaged, which gives it a long life. Pasteurization provides a product with an average shelf life of 7-10 days. Raw milk is associated with pathogenic diseases such as tuberculosis, brucellosis and typhoid fever, which is why heat treatment is necessary.

subjective.question: How are curd, paneer and cheese prepared from milk?
subjective.answer: Curd (yoghurt): lactic acid bacteria (LAB) produce lactic acid and are used as a starter culture for the production of yoghurt from milk; when the pH reaches 4.6, the milk protein casein coagulates as curd, and the optimum temperature for curd formation is 35-40°C. Paneer: it is prepared by adding lemon juice or citric acid to hot milk and precipitating the casein; paneer contains about 18 percent protein. Cheese: the formed cheese is coated with paraffin to prevent loss of moisture and allowed to ripen at low temperature; cheese contains about 24 percent protein and is thus a concentrated source of protein.

subjective.question: Describe the composition of meat and the changes that take place in it after slaughter.
subjective.answer: The average protein content of meat ranges from 16 to 23 percent and the average fat content from 10 to 40 percent. In muscle tissue the smallest unit is the muscle fiber, and the fat distributed in the lean part of meat is called marbling. Myoglobin is the pigment that gives meat its red colour; on refrigeration it changes to brown-red, and on heating to grayish brown. After slaughter, oxidation of glycogen produces lactic acid, and swelling of muscle fibers with fluid makes the meat hard - this is called rigor mortis. The stiff muscles start softening after holding for some time; this process is called aging. Fresh meat is stored at a refrigeration temperature of 2 to 5°C.

subjective.question: Describe the structure of a cereal grain and name the most common cereals.
subjective.answer: A cereal grain (kernel) consists of the bran, the germ and the endosperm. Bran is the outer chaffy coat that covers the kernel. The germ is a small structure at the lower end of the endosperm. The endosperm constitutes about 84-85% of the kernel. The most common cereal foods are rice, wheat and maize (maize is also called corn). Cereals contain 65-75% carbohydrates; rice contains about 78% carbohydrates. Malt, used in the brewing industry, converts the starches present in barley, rye, rice, corn or other grains to maltose, which yeast utilizes to produce ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide.

subjective.question: What is food spoilage? Which organisms and processes are involved in it?
subjective.answer: Spoilage is defined as undesirable changes in the properties of a product. Lipolysis is the breakdown of fats and other lipids by hydrolysis to release fatty acids. Pigment-forming bacteria include Flavobacterium, Micrococcus and Serratia, while a beverage can swells due to the activity of Clostridium botulinum. The best pH for the growth of microorganisms is 7. Psychrotrophs grow at 5°C or less and make up a large number of the microbes in milk, so chilling/refrigeration limits the spoilage rate because temperatures below the optimal range inhibit microbial growth and enzymatic as well as chemical reactions.

subjective.question: Write a note on enzymes in foods: proteases, amylases and diastatic power.
subjective.answer: Proteases are enzymes that degrade proteins; examples of protein enzymes in food processing are the proteolytic enzymes used in the tenderization of meats, pectinases in the ripening of fruits, and trypsin inhibitors found in legume seeds. Amylases act on starch: the amylase activity in milk is often referred to as diastatic power and refers to the production of reducing substances by the action of alpha and beta amylases. Sugars can be detected because they react with the anthrone reagent under acidic conditions to yield a blue-green colour.
